A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same compression framework and retain corresponding algorithms, theoretical results, and experiments. The complete main texts, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression-error simulations and neural-network experiments in Figures 2–5, including teacher–student dataset compression and cylindrical-harmonic regression.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds runtime measurements, attention-head compression experiments, and numerical tests of polylogarithmic compression in Figures 6–8.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects the cluster-diameter condition from dependence on the original d to dependence on the current active support size. This aligns the pseudocode with the active-set argument already present in v1 Appendix A.5. The moment-matching procedure, hybrid clustering implementation, and gradient rescaling remain unchanged; attention experiments apply the existing framework.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix F adds episodic in-context regression on random piecewise-linear functions using causal multi-head attention, substantially extending the earlier fixed-function, two-layer-network tasks. Appendix G also adds a reciprocal-function compression test. The original synthetic tasks remain.

E2.justification: The comparisons retain full, uncompressed models or datasets and naive random subsets as controls. The new attention experiment uses the corresponding full model and randomly selected heads, extending the same comparator strategy to the new task. No additional competing compression method is evaluated.

E3.justification: The retained experiments keep their settings. New protocols include compressing 4000 attention heads to 800 with order-3 matching, then training with Adam at learning rate 0.0001 and batch size 256 for 50 epochs of five steps. Figures 6 and 8 add runtime measurements across dimensions and an order search for compression to 120 log d or 20 log-squared d objects.

E4.justification: v2 adds systematic runtime scaling with object count and dimension in Figure 6, and directly examines the feasibility of polylogarithmic compression in Figure 8 by searching moment-matching orders. These address computational cost and a substantially stronger compression regime than the retained fixed-fraction and square-root compression experiments.

E5.justification: The existing 20-trial reporting for Figure 2 and 10-instance reporting for Figure 5 remain unchanged, including standard-deviation error bars. v2 additionally specifies five-trial averages and standard deviations for the new Figures 6 and 8. This adds repetition information without indicating increased repetitions for existing experiments.

E6.justification: Figures 2–5 retain their plotted results, including Figure 5's exponents 0.683 versus 1.271 and 0.308 versus 0.607. New results show approximately linear runtime scaling, close correspondence between the 4000-head model and its 800-head compressed version, and generally decreasing compression errors at polylogarithmic target sizes. These are additional findings, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: New Appendix B introduces quasi-uniformity, a polynomial superlevel-set lemma, and Theorem 8 claiming an optimal compression lower bound. v2 also changes the achievable-size statements in Theorems 4 and 7 from Omega to O, revises the Appendix A.2 uniqueness argument, and makes boundedness and regularity conditions explicit in Theorem 5. The new lower-bound lemma has a mathematical defect, detailed in the overall assessment.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction newly claim that polylogarithmic compression is optimal up to a constant factor, extending v1's achievability claim to an optimality claim. The introduction also explicitly qualifies the relevant symmetric functions as smooth. The main dynamical-LTH and improved-scaling-law contributions otherwise remain.

C2.justification: Section 5 newly acknowledges that the compressed-width scaling for deep networks remains open and that regularity of the training-composed function does not automatically follow from regularity of the model. v2 also discusses empirical applicability to nonsmooth ReLU networks, possible smoothness degradation at high dimension, and oscillations in the new polylogarithmic-compression results. These materially qualify the framework's applicability.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproducibility statement providing a repository address for the compression implementation and figure-generation code; v1 provides no corresponding access information. It also documents Apple M4 Pro timing hardware and detailed generation, architecture, and training settings for the attention experiment. Repository availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Pensia et al. (2021), Brudnyi and Yomdin (2015), Du and Tanaka-Ishii (2025), and Yang and Zhou (2025). These support the LTH discussion, new lower-bound argument, and expanded discussion of intrinsic dimension and approximation rates. The broader positioning relative to compression and scaling-law research remains.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, updates author information, copyedits passages, and presents existing regularity conditions as a numbered assumption. It adds topical appendices, reproducibility and language-model-use statements, and renumbers retained appendices. The main section sequence and most existing exposition remain recognizable rather than being extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR conference layout, changing typography, headers, title presentation, figure sizing, and placement; Figures 2 and 3 now share a page. Three new figures display runtime, attention, and polylogarithmic-compression results. The revised captions for Figures 3 and 4 incorrectly swap the blue and green curve descriptions while the plotted curves remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful experiments, reproducibility information, and important applicability qualifications. However, its new headline optimality claim relies on Appendix B Lemma 2, whose Equation 57 is false as written: for D = [-1,1], p(x) = x, k = 1, and t = 1/2, the superlevel-volume fraction is 1/2, whereas the stated bound requires at least 3/4. This substantive proof problem, alongside the new caption errors, offsets clear benefits sufficiently that a reliable net quality direction cannot be established.
